findings.docQuote: `start` has no Safari path. Passing `--browser safari` (or `webkit-based`) exits with `E_UNSUPPORTED_BROWSER`.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension start ./scratch-ext --browser safari --no-browser --output json   (extension@4.1.3)
findings.observed: {"schema":1,"ok":false,"command":"start","status":"usage","value":null,"error":{"code":"E_COMMAND_UNSUPPORTED_FOR_TARGET","message":"Safari is not supported by start."},"warnings":[]}  — identical output for --browser webkit-based. E_UNSUPPORTED_BROWSER does exist elsewhere in the bundle (24 occurrences) but is not the code emitted here.
findings.why: This page is the machine-output reference for `start`, and the surrounding section tells agents and CI scripts to branch on error codes. Anything matching on E_UNSUPPORTED_BROWSER will silently fail to recognize the Safari rejection and fall through to a generic failure path.

findings.docQuote: The template wires up `manifest.json`, popup, and content script entry points so you can run `extension dev` and start iterating immediately.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension create scratch-ext --output json  then  find scratch-ext/src -type f  and  grep -ri popup scratch-ext/src/
findings.observed: src/ contains background.js, content/ContentApp.js, content/scripts.js, content/styles.css, images/icon.png, manifest.json, sidebar/SidebarApp.js, sidebar/index.html, sidebar/scripts.js, sidebar/styles.css. grep for 'popup' returns nothing. The manifest declares chromium:side_panel / firefox:sidebar_action and an action with only default_title ("Open Side Panel"), no default_popup. The template's own package.json description is "Adds a sidebar panel to the browser with a simple page."
findings.why: The page's entire "What you get" section is the reason to pick this template. A reader expecting popup wiring scaffolds the project, opens src/, and finds a sidebar app instead, with no popup entrypoint anywhere. The frontmatter description repeats the same wrong claim, so it also surfaces in search results.

findings.docQuote: If your project lacks optional refresh dependencies, Extension.js installs them and asks for a restart.
findings.evidence: /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/programs/develop/plugin-js-frameworks/js-tools/react.ts lines 14-17 and 103-113, plus programs/develop/lib/optional-deps-resolver.ts line 584
findings.observed: react.ts imports and calls only resolveOptionalContractPackageWithoutInstall and loadOptionalContractModuleWithoutInstall for contractId 'react-refresh'. The resolver's failure path is `throw new Error(formatResolverError({... installSpecs ...}))` — it formats an install hint for the detected package manager and aborts. grep across programs/develop finds no auto-install call for optional deps and no "restart" message. The page itself says the opposite 14 lines earlier: "When one is missing, the build error names the exact version that matches the bundled toolchain."
findings.why: A reader whose build aborts on a missing react-refresh will wait for an install that never runs, or assume the abort is a bug rather than the instruction to install the package themselves. The two statements on the same page also disagree, so there is no way to tell which behavior to expect.

findings.docQuote: The catalog holds 52 templates in 6 groups: starters, sidebar, content scripts, new tab, toolbar action, and special folders.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension create --help   and   ./node_modules/.bin/extension --ai-help --output json | python3 -c "...len(d['templates']['names'])"   (extension@4.1.3)
findings.observed: `create --help` prints the header "Templates (53)" and the ai-help JSON reports len(templates.names) == 53. Counting the six groups the help prints: starters 7, sidebar 11, content scripts 16, new tab 15, toolbar action 2, special folders 2 = 53. The group names and count of 6 are correct.
findings.why: The number is the one concrete fact in that sentence and it is off by one against what the CLI prints, so a reader comparing the page against `create --help` cannot tell whether the docs or the CLI is behind.

findings.docQuote: icons/<filename>
findings.evidence: Built scratch-ext with ./node_modules/.bin/extension start ./scratch-ext --no-browser, then inspected dist/chromium/manifest.json and the emitted tree; cross-checked /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/programs/develop/plugin-web-extension/feature-icons/steps/emit-file.ts lines 245-274
findings.observed: The source manifest declares icons and action.default_icon as "images/icon.png". The build emitted dist/chromium/images/icon.png and the output manifest still points at "images/icon.png" — nothing under an icons/ folder. emit-file.ts sets outputDir='icons' and then immediately overrides it: "Icons keep their manifest-relative location so they can't collide with another emitted asset that owns icons/<basename>", replacing filename with the path relative to the manifest directory.
findings.why: The "Output path" section is where someone goes to predict emitted asset paths for packaging scripts or web_accessible_resources entries. Icons are emitted at their manifest-relative source location, so a script that looks under dist/<browser>/icons/ finds nothing unless the source folder happened to be named icons/.

findings.docQuote:
Your repository includes an E2E workflow example at:

- `.github/workflows/e2e.yml`
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension create scratch-ext  then  ls -a scratch-ext
findings.observed: A freshly scaffolded project contains .extension-create.json, .extension-js, .git, .gitignore, README.md, STORE.md, extension.config.js, package.json, src/ — there is no .github directory at all. The file .github/workflows/e2e.yml exists only in the extension.js framework repository itself, which is not the reader's repository.
findings.why: The page addresses the reader's own extension project throughout, so this reads as a promise that scaffolding gave them a working E2E workflow to copy. They will look for a file that was never created and have no pointer to the real example.

findings.docQuote: ## Video walkthrough
findings.evidence: sed -n '41,47p' /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/_FUTURE/extension.js.org/docs/features/index.mdx
findings.observed: The heading is immediately followed by "## Next steps" on line 43 with only a blank line between. No <Frame>, no iframe, no link — the section is empty. Sibling pages in the same docs set (for example docs/languages-and-frameworks/react.mdx line 263) put a real youtube-nocookie <Frame> under the same heading.
findings.why: The heading advertises a walkthrough video that the rendered page does not contain, so a reader looking for the visual explanation scrolls past an empty section and assumes the page failed to load.

findings.docQuote: If your project lacks Sass tooling, Extension.js installs the optional dependencies and asks for a restart.
findings.evidence: Added `import './extra.scss'` to the scaffolded preact template with no `sass` in package.json, then ran `./node_modules/.bin/extension build` and `./node_modules/.bin/extension dev --no-browser` (extension@4.1.3). Message source: missingSassDependency / preprocessor-passthrough-loader.mjs in node_modules/extension-develop/dist.
findings.observed: Both commands completed with a warning and installed nothing (`ls node_modules/sass` -> No such file or directory afterwards, package.json unchanged): "This Sass/SCSS file shipped uncompiled. The sass package isn't installed in this project. The raw Sass/SCSS source was copied as-is into the output .css. Browsers treat it as broken CSS, so those surfaces render unstyled. Install it to compile this file: npm install --save-dev sass". No restart was requested. After `npm install --save-dev sass` the same build emitted `.sasstest{color:#64ff00}` correctly.
findings.why: A reader who trusts this note will skip installing sass and assume the toolchain handles it. The build still succeeds, so the failure is silent: raw SCSS is copied into the output .css and every surface using it renders unstyled in the shipped extension.

findings.docQuote:
Install the required dependencies:

```bash npm
npm install -D sass sass-loader
```
findings.evidence: `sass-loader` is a direct dependency of extension-develop: package-lock.json in the scratch project shows node_modules/extension-develop requiring sass-loader 17.0.0. The CLI's own missing-dependency message names only `sass` ("Add it to your devDependencies: npm install --save-dev sass"). Verified by installing only `sass` and rebuilding.
findings.observed: With devDependencies of only {sass ^1.103.1, extension ^4.1.3, ...} and no user-installed sass-loader, `extension build` compiled the .scss correctly (`grep -o 'sasstest{[^}]*}' dist/chromium/sidebar/index.css` -> `sasstest{color:#64ff00}`).
findings.why: Only `sass` is required. Telling readers to add `sass-loader` to their own devDependencies adds a package the toolchain already pins at 17.0.0, inviting a version that disagrees with the bundled rspack loader chain.

findings.docQuote: `excludeBrowserFlags` removes user flags by prefix matching.
findings.evidence: Both the Firefox and Chromium launch paths call the same helper. node_modules/extension/dist/browsers.cjs: run-firefox `browserConfig` does `filterBrowserFlags((browserFlags||[]).map(String), excludeFlags)`, and the Chromium path does `filterBrowserFlags(DEFAULT_BROWSER_FLAGS, excludeFlags)`. The helper is: `flags.filter((flag)=>!excludeFlags.some((excludeFlag)=>{ if(!excludeFlag) return false; if(flag===excludeFlag) return true; return flag.startsWith(`${excludeFlag}=`)||flag.startsWith(`${excludeFlag},`); }))`
findings.observed: Matching is exact, or the exclude value followed by `=` or `,`. It is not prefix matching: `excludeBrowserFlags: ['--dev']` does not remove `--devtools`. Conversely the Chromium description one bullet up (line 154, "exact-match filtering") understates the same helper, which also strips `--disable-features=Translate` when you exclude `--disable-features`.
findings.why: The page describes two different matching rules for two browser families that in fact share one implementation. A Firefox user following the documented prefix rule will write a short exclude value, see the flag still passed to the binary, and have no way to tell from the docs why.

findings.docQuote: Popup, options, and content scripts ship as React entry points with hot module replacement (HMR) wired up.
findings.evidence: /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/_FUTURE/examples/examples/react/src/manifest.json and `find react/src -type f`
findings.observed: The react template manifest declares chromium:action (title only, no default_popup), chromium:side_panel / firefox:sidebar_action, background, and content_scripts. There is no action.default_popup, no options_ui and no options_page key. The src tree is background.ts, sidebar/{index.html,scripts.tsx,styles.css,SidebarApp.tsx}, content/{scripts.tsx,ContentApp.tsx,styles.css}. package.json description: "Adds a sidebar panel to the browser with a simple React page."
findings.why: A reader picks --template=react expecting popup and options React entry points and gets a sidebar extension instead, then has to author the popup and options surfaces from scratch.

findings.docQuote: src="/images/examples/new-react/screenshot.png"
findings.evidence: python3 -c on examples/react/package.json and examples/new-react/package.json
findings.observed: react -> "Adds a sidebar panel to the browser with a simple React page."; new-react -> "Replaces your new tab page with a simple React page." The page for --template=react embeds the screenshot of the separate new-react template (a new-tab page), labelled alt="React template preview".
findings.why: The preview image shows a new-tab page, so the reader forms the wrong expectation of what --template=react produces before they scaffold it.

findings.docQuote: Vanilla JavaScript extension with a new-tab page.
findings.evidence: grep -c newtab /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/_FUTURE/examples/examples/javascript/src/manifest.json
findings.observed: 0 matches. The manifest keys are chromium:action, firefox:browser_action, chromium:side_panel, firefox:sidebar_action, background, content_scripts (no chrome_url_overrides). The src tree is background.js, sidebar/, content/, images/. package.json and README both say "Adds a sidebar panel to the browser with a simple page."
findings.why: A reader who wants a new-tab starter scaffolds --template=javascript and gets a sidebar plus content script, with no new-tab override anywhere in the project.

findings.evidence: examples/new-svelte/package.json pins "svelte": "^5.15.0"; examples/new-svelte/src/newtab/scripts.ts and examples/content-svelte/src/content/scripts.ts both use `import {mount} from 'svelte'` then `mount(App, {target})`. grep of node_modules/svelte@5.56.10/src/internal/client/errors.js line 103.
findings.observed: Svelte 5 throws on the documented call: "component_api_invalid_new: Attempted to instantiate ${component} with `new ${name}`, which is no longer valid in Svelte 5. If this component is not under your control, set the `compatibility.componentApi` compiler option to `4` to keep it working." The same applies to the `app.$destroy()` teardown on line 201. Both shipped Svelte templates use mount() instead.
findings.why: A reader copying either example into a project that installed current Svelte (which is what the templates and `npm install svelte` give them) gets a runtime error and a blank UI, with nothing on the page explaining that the API shown is Svelte 4 only.

findings.docQuote: | `chrome_url_overrides.newtab`  | `/src/newtab.html`         | `newtab/index.html`             |
findings.evidence: Built a project whose manifest declares "chrome_url_overrides": {"newtab": "/src/newtab.html"} with `./node_modules/.bin/extension build ./proj --browser=chrome`, then read proj/dist/chrome/manifest.json
findings.observed: "chrome_url_overrides": { "newtab": "chrome_url_overrides/newtab.html" }, and the emitted tree contains chrome_url_overrides/newtab.html. There is no newtab/ directory in dist/chrome. Every other row of the table reproduced exactly (action/index.html, background/service_worker.js, background/index.html, content_scripts/content-0.js, content_scripts/content-0.css, devtools/index.html, options/index.html, sandbox/page-0.html, sidebar/index.html from both side_panel and sidebar_action, storage/managed_schema.json, user_scripts/api_script.js).
findings.why: This table is the page's reference payload. A reader who hardcodes newtab/index.html in chrome.runtime.getURL, a web_accessible_resources entry, or a test assertion points at a file that is never emitted.

findings.docQuote: Output: `chrome-extension:<extension-id>/icons/icon.png`
findings.evidence: Chrome extension URL scheme; the built asset lands at dist/chrome/icons/icon.png per the build tree above.
findings.observed: chrome.runtime.getURL returns a URL of the form chrome-extension://<extension-id>/icons/icon.png. The documented string omits the // authority separator, so it is not a valid extension URL.
findings.why: A reader who copies the shown form when hand-building or asserting on an extension URL produces a string the browser will not resolve.

findings.docQuote: Values that are not hex strings pass through untouched.
findings.evidence: parseCssThemeColor and patchChromiumThemeColors in node_modules/extension-develop/dist/0~rspack-config.mjs
findings.observed: patchChromiumThemeColors calls parseCssThemeColor, not parseHexThemeColor. parseCssThemeColor also converts the keyword "transparent" to [0,0,0,0], any of the ~148 entries in the bundled NAMED_CSS_COLORS table (for example "tomato" to [255,99,71]), and rgb()/rgba() strings via /^rgba?\(\s*(\d{1,3})...\)$/. Only strings none of those match are left as-is.
findings.why: A reader concludes that only hex is portable and avoids writing named or rgb() colors in theme.colors, or wrongly expects a named color to reach Chrome verbatim and be rejected, when the build actually converts it for them.

findings.docQuote: Extension.js can detect Stylelint configuration files for diagnostics/reporting, but it does not inject Stylelint into the build pipeline.
findings.evidence: grep -ril stylelint node_modules/extension node_modules/extension-develop node_modules/extension-create; grep -ro 'stylelintrc' over the same dist trees
findings.observed: The only stylelint hits in the shipped CLI are node_modules/extension-develop/README.md and two occurrences inside node_modules/extension/dist/cli.cjs, both of which are the literal template name 'new-config-stylelint' in the template catalog. There is no reference to .stylelintrc, stylelint.config, or any stylelint config lookup anywhere in the shipped code.
findings.why: A reader expects Extension.js to surface stylelint diagnostics during dev or build and waits for reporting that the CLI has no code to produce.

findings.docQuote: `--format` is a deprecated alias for `--output`. It still works, and the CLI prints a deprecation warning on stderr once per run. The same applies to the older `--wait-format` alias.
findings.evidence: cd <sandbox>/scratch && ../node_modules/.bin/extension build . --format json 2>/dev/null   (compared against: extension build . --output json 2>/dev/null, and extension create ../fmtprobe4 --format json 2>/dev/null)
findings.observed: `build --format json` printed the normal pretty build card ("🧩 Extension.js 4.1.3 ... Extension built for production in dist/chromium") and nothing on stderr; `--format=json` behaved the same. `build --output json` printed {"schema":1,"ok":true,"command":"build",...}. `create --format json` likewise printed the pretty card and ended with "3. npm run dev", while `create --output json` ended with {"schema":1,"ok":true,"command":"create",...}. The deprecation warning appears only for `--ai-help` (extension dev --ai-help --format json prints "--format is deprecated and maps to --output."). The flag is accepted (an unknown flag like --bogus errors out) but silently ignored on real commands.
findings.why: A CI script or agent that follows this page and passes `--format json` to build, create, start or preview gets human-formatted output with no envelope and no warning that anything was ignored, so its JSON parse fails with no clue why. The page presents `--format` as a working global alias when it only works for `--ai-help`.

findings.docQuote: - `.ts` source files with no `tsconfig.json` is a hard error. Create the file next to `package.json` to fix it.
findings.evidence: Built a minimal project with package.json, manifest.json declaring background.ts, one background.ts, and no tsconfig.json: ../node_modules/.bin/extension build .
findings.observed: Exit code 0. Output: "⏵⏵⏵ Creating a default tsconfig.json… / ⏵⏵⏵ Writing the type definitions for tsprobe… / ⏵⏵⏵ Extension built for production in dist/chromium (161 B)." A tsconfig.json was written into the project. The shipped code path (extension-develop/dist/839.mjs) reads `if (hasDep || hasTsFiles) { if (tsConfigFilePath) {...} else { writeTsConfig(projectPath) } }` — there is no error branch.
findings.why: A reader is told .ts without a tsconfig fails the build, so they will add a manual gate or a pre-step in CI to prevent an error that never happens, and will not expect the CLI to silently write a tsconfig.json into their repo (which it does).

findings.docQuote: Set `hashContentScripts: false` in `extension.config.*` to opt out and keep stable dev filenames.
findings.evidence: Two dev runs on the same project, only extension.config.js differing. (a) `export default {hashContentScripts: false}` then `extension dev . --no-browser --browser=chrome`; (b) `export default {commands: {dev: {hashContentScripts: false}}}` then the same command. Config typings at node_modules/extension/dist/extension/config-types.d.ts declare hashContentScripts only on DevCommandConfig, never on FileConfig.
findings.observed: (a) top-level: dist/chrome/content_scripts/content-0.e455cb80.js — still hashed, no warning. (b) commands.dev: dist/chrome/content_scripts/content-0.js — hash gone. The key is only honored under `commands.dev`.
findings.why: The page names the file but not the nesting, and the most literal reading (a top-level key in extension.config.js) is silently ignored, so a reader who wants stable dev filenames sets it, sees hashed filenames anyway, and has no error to tell them the key landed in the wrong place.

findings.docQuote:
src="/images/examples/new-svelte/screenshot.png"
  alt="Svelte template preview"
findings.evidence: ls images/examples | grep -i svelte  →  content-svelte, new-svelte (no `svelte` dir). The template this page scaffolds is examples/svelte, whose src/manifest.json reads "name": "Svelte Sidebar Example", "description": "Adds a sidebar panel to the browser with a simple Svelte page." and declares chromium:action / firefox:browser_action "Open Side Panel". examples/svelte/screenshot.png exists in the examples repo but is not mirrored into images/examples/.
findings.observed: The image labelled "Svelte template preview" is new-svelte's screenshot (the new-tab-page template), not the sidebar extension that `extension create my-extension --template=svelte` actually produces.
findings.why: The only visual on the page shows a different extension from the one the command on the same page creates, so a reader picks the template expecting the pictured new-tab UI and gets a side-panel extension instead.

findings.docQuote: ## Video walkthrough
findings.evidence:
sed -n '228,231p' docs/languages-and-frameworks/typescript.mdx | od -c  →  the file ends '...cross-browser-compatibility).

## Video walkthrough

' (231 lines total, nothing after the heading).
findings.observed: The final section heading has no body: no <Frame>, no iframe, no link. Every other video-bearing page in this batch (browser-profile, debugging, reload-and-hmr, tailwindcss) embeds a youtube-nocookie iframe under its Frame.
findings.why: The page advertises a video walkthrough that does not exist, so a reader scrolls to the bottom looking for it and finds an empty section.

findings.docQuote:
In content scripts, Extension.js emits CSS as stylesheet content without JavaScript class-name mappings.

Use component-level local class naming in content scripts. Do not assume CSS module class imports work there unless you have explicitly tested it.
findings.evidence: Copied the official content-css-modules template src/ into a scratch project and ran `./node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chromium --silent` with extension@4.1.3, then read dist/chromium/content_scripts/content-0.js and content-0.css.
findings.observed: The content-script bundle contains a JS class-name map: `t.exports={Kc:"PXCbrW",Qv:"tfIcXq",F1:"T6jGon",bW:"pGoVxa"}` and the emitted CSS uses the matching hashed selectors (`.PXCbrW{color:#0a0c10;...}`). The template's own src/content/scripts.js imports named exports from './styles.module.css' and assigns them to className.
findings.why: The page tells readers a working feature does not work, and it does so a few lines after recommending the content-css-modules template, which depends on exactly that feature. A reader following the note will hand-write global class names in content scripts and reintroduce the collisions CSS modules exist to prevent.

findings.docQuote: Extension.js sets `type: "module"` automatically when your background entry uses ES module syntax.
findings.evidence: In a scaffolded project, replaced src/background.js with `import {greet} from "./helper.js"` (plus a helper module) and ran `./node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chromium --silent`, then printed the `background` block of dist/chromium/manifest.json. Also grepped the whole installed extension@4.1.3 and extension-develop trees: no code path assigns background.type = "module"; patchBackground only spreads the author's existing background object.
findings.observed: Emitted manifest background block: {"service_worker": "background/service_worker.js"} — no `type` key at all, despite the entry using a static ES `import`.
findings.why: The page presents this as the reason a reader does not need to add `type: "module"` themselves. The same claim is repeated in the 'How Extension.js helps' list at line 122. A reader debugging a worker that needs a real module context will look for a setting the tool never writes.

findings.docQuote: If your project lacks optional Vue tooling, Extension.js installs it and asks for a restart.
findings.evidence: Created a project with only `vue` in dependencies (npm i vue@^3.4.0, no vue-loader) and an App.vue import, then ran `./node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chromium`. Also read the shipped resolver in node_modules/extension-develop/dist/0~rspack-config.mjs (ensureOptionalPackageResolved / formatResolverError).
findings.observed: The build completed with no install and no restart prompt; the project's package.json and node_modules were unchanged and vue-loader was never added (it resolved from the CLI's own dependency tree). Where the package genuinely cannot be resolved, the shipped code throws: `[${integration}] ${headline} Install it with: ${hint}` — an error with an install hint, never an automatic install.
findings.why: It contradicts line 149 on the same page ('the build error names the exact version that matches the bundled toolchain') and the troubleshooting entry at line 168 ('Prompt to restart after install'). A reader who hits a missing-tooling error will wait for an install that never happens instead of running the install command the error printed.

findings.docQuote: Static types across popup, content, and background scripts, with `chrome` and `browser` API typings configured.
findings.evidence: Ran `./node_modules/.bin/extension create ts-check --template=typescript` with extension@4.1.3, then `find ts-check/src -type f` and `grep -c popup ts-check/src/manifest.json`.
findings.observed: Scaffolded files: src/background.ts, src/content/{ContentApp.ts,scripts.ts,styles.css,types.d.ts}, src/sidebar/{SidebarApp.ts,index.html,scripts.ts,styles.css}, src/manifest.json, src/images/icon.png. grep for 'popup' in the manifest returns 0. The manifest declares chromium:side_panel / firefox:sidebar_action and an action whose default_title is 'Open Side Panel' with no default_popup; the template is named 'TypeScript Sidebar Example'.
findings.why: The page's frontmatter description also promises 'pre-wired popup, content, and background script entry points'. A reader choosing this template to start a popup-based extension gets a sidebar template with no popup surface and has to wire the popup themselves.

findings.docQuote: src="/images/examples/new-typescript/screenshot.png"
findings.evidence: `ls images/examples/ | grep -i typescript` in the docs repo, plus `extension create --help` template listing.
findings.observed: images/examples/ contains new-typescript and content-typescript but no `typescript` directory. `new-typescript` is listed under the 'New tab (replaces the browser new tab page)' group in the CLI catalog, while every create command on this page scaffolds `--template=typescript`, which is a sidebar starter.
findings.why: The preview labelled 'TypeScript template preview' shows a different template's new-tab UI than the one the page's commands scaffold, so a reader forms the wrong expectation of what they will get before they even run create.

findings.docQuote: | `scripts/`    | Adds script files to compilation as entrypoints, even when no manifest or HTML entry references them.       |
findings.evidence: Created scripts/injected.js (a default-export mount function) in a scaffolded project and ran `./node_modules/.bin/extension build`. Then appended the literal string `// reference: scripts/injected.js` to src/background.js and ran the identical build again. Root cause is programs/develop/plugin-special-folders/get-data.ts:230 `filterUnreferencedScripts` ("Keep a scripts/ entry only if the extension actually references it (manifest, HTML, or runtime string path)"), which drops any entry whose project-relative path is not a substring of the source corpus.
findings.observed: Build 1 (unreferenced) emitted no scripts/ output at all: dist/chromium contained content_scripts/, assets/, images/, sidebar/, manifest.json, background/, _locales/, pages/, vendor/ and nothing else, total 35.9 KB. Build 2, differing only by the reference string, emitted `scripts/injected.js (8.11KB)` and totalled 44.0 KB. No warning or error was printed in build 1.
findings.why: A reader puts a dynamically-injected script in scripts/ precisely because nothing references it statically, ships the build, and the file is silently absent from dist. The failure is invisible at build time and only surfaces as a runtime 404 from chrome.scripting.executeScript.

findings.docQuote:
Boot a session, fire the action, and assert on the side effect, with no browser UI and no Playwright. This is the whole loop in a GitHub Actions job:

```yaml
- run: pnpm extension dev --browser=chromium --allow-control --wait --output json
findings.evidence: Ran `./node_modules/.bin/extension dev --browser=chromium --allow-control --wait --wait-timeout 6000 --output json` in a built project with no dev session running. programs/extension/commands/dev.ts:350-395 shows the `--wait` branch calls runWaitMode() and returns before any server is started; programs/extension/commands/dev-wait.ts only polls for a ready.json another process must write.
findings.observed: Exit code 1. stdout: {"schema":1,"ok":false,"command":"dev","status":"timeout","value":null,"error":{"code":"E_READY_TIMEOUT","message":"Timed out waiting for ready contract at .../dist/extension-js/chromium/ready.json (6000 ms)"},"warnings":[],"hint":"Raise --wait-timeout, or read the server output for what kept it from reporting ready."}
findings.why: `--wait` is a readiness gate, not a launcher, so the first CI step boots nothing and fails with E_READY_TIMEOUT after the 60s default. A reader copying this job gets a red pipeline at step 1 and no indication that a backgrounded `extension dev` is the missing piece.

findings.docQuote: A non-default binary adds a Binary row, and `build` swaps the Profile and Run ID rows for an Output row.
findings.evidence: programs/extension/browsers/browsers-lib/messages.ts:1106-1109 comments the card row list with "No Binary row in any case. A pinned run says so in the Browser row, and the path the user typed is the path they typed", and the row array contains only Browser / Extension / Profile / Run ID / Extension ID. programs/extension/browsers/__spec__/card-binary-provenance.spec.ts asserts `expect(card).not.toContain('Binary')` for managed, unknown, pinned (--chromium-binary), system and snapshot provenance.
findings.observed: No Binary row exists in any code path. For a pinned binary the spec asserts the card reads `Browser        Chromium 139.0.7259.2 (pinned with --chromium-binary)` and still contains no 'Binary' string. (The second half of the sentence is correct: my `extension build` printed Browser / Extension / Output with no Profile or Run ID row.)
findings.why: A reader running with --chromium-binary or --gecko-binary looks for a Binary row to confirm which binary launched, never finds one, and may conclude the flag was ignored. The real signal is the parenthetical on the Browser row, which the page never mentions.

findings.docQuote: A progressive setup with `.vue` single-file components, ready for popup, options, and content-script contexts.
findings.evidence: The `vue` template source at /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/_FUTURE/examples/examples/vue: `find src -type f` and `cat src/manifest.json`. `extension create --help` also files `vue` under "Starters (a bare manifest, or one language or framework with sidebar UI)", not under any popup/options group.
findings.observed: src/ contains background.ts, content/{ContentApp.vue,scripts.ts,styles.css,types.d.ts}, images/icon.png, manifest.json, sidebar/{SidebarApp.vue,index.html,scripts.ts,styles.css}. The manifest is named "Vue Sidebar Example" and declares chromium:side_panel / firefox:sidebar_action plus content_scripts. There is no default_popup, no options_ui and no options_page anywhere in the template.
findings.why: A reader picking `--template=vue` for a popup or options-page extension scaffolds a sidebar extension instead and has to build both surfaces by hand, having been told they were already wired up.

findings.docQuote:
src="/images/examples/new-vue/screenshot.png"
  alt="Vue template preview"
findings.evidence: `md5 -q _FUTURE/examples/examples/vue/screenshot.png _FUTURE/examples/examples/new-vue/screenshot.png _FUTURE/extension.js.org/images/examples/new-vue/screenshot.png` and `ls images/examples/vue`.
findings.observed: vue/screenshot.png = 50ae837f3c2c1fd5147bbd91d443e4a9; new-vue/screenshot.png = 4038bbbdef3717783fac78a29372e7c5; the image the page loads = 4038bbbdef3717783fac78a29372e7c5, i.e. the new-vue image. `images/examples/vue` does not exist in the site repo, so the vue template's own screenshot was never published.
findings.why: The page labelled "Vue browser extension template" shows the new-vue (new-tab-page) template's screenshot as its "Vue template preview", so the reader's expectation of what `--template=vue` produces is set by a different template.

findings.docQuote: | Pages / UI (popup, options, sidebar, devtools, new tab) | 1 MiB          | Opened on demand.                                          |
findings.evidence: programs/develop/plugin-perf-budgets/categorize.ts defines AssetCategory as 'content-script' | 'service-worker' | 'page' | 'runtime' | 'ignored', with BUDGET_BYTES = {'content-script': 512*1024, 'service-worker': 512*1024, page: 1024*1024, runtime: 1024*1024, ignored: Infinity}. `runtime` catches root-level assets and every `.wasm` file: "Hashed wasm cores and sibling runtime helpers (ffmpeg, tesseract, …) emit at the output root, not under a named surface folder."
findings.observed: Four finite budget categories exist and can warn; the page's table lists three and its `perfBudgets` override example only shows 'content-script', 'service-worker' and page.
findings.why: A project with a large wasm core gets a budget warning attributed to a category the page never names, and a reader following the override example has no documented key to raise it, since `runtime` is missing from both the table and the snippet.

findings.docQuote: ## Video walkthrough
findings.evidence:
`wc -l docs/browsers/index.mdx` reports 67 lines; `tail -3 docs/browsers/index.mdx | od -c` shows the file ends with "
 # #   V i d e o   w a l k t h r o u g h 
 
" and nothing else. Sibling pages such as docs/commands/inspect.mdx and docs/features/special-folders.mdx embed a real <Frame><iframe src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/..."> under their video sections.

findings.why: The reader is promised a video walkthrough at the end of the browser-targeting guide and gets an empty section, with no way to tell whether the video failed to load or was never there.

findings.docQuote: In development builds only, the compiler warns when the emitted manifest still contains one of these deprecated generated paths:
findings.evidence: Built a project whose manifest.json sets "devtools_page": "devtools_page/devtools_page.html", then ran: ./node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser chrome  (production mode, the default). Source: programs/develop/plugin-web-extension/feature-manifest/steps/legacy-warnings.ts:21 comment reads "Production builds never consult this set so a single build always surfaces every hit."
findings.observed: The production build printed the warning: "The devtools_page field uses a deprecated scaffold path. / PATH devtools_page/devtools_page.html / Point it at devtools/index.html, Extension.js already emits the page there." followed by "legacy audit compiled with warnings in 26 ms." The `isDev` check in legacy-warnings.ts only controls per-session deduplication, not whether the warning is emitted.
findings.why: A reader who sees this warning in CI output from `extension build` will think something is misconfigured about their build mode, or will assume the docs mean the warning cannot appear in a release build and go looking for a different cause. It also understates the reach of the deprecation: production builds surface every hit, not none.

findings.docQuote: When a project has a `package.json`, Extension.js ignores `public/manifest.json`. This prevents a copied static asset from overwriting the manifest that Extension.js generates.
findings.evidence: In a project with a package.json, copied the source manifest to public/manifest.json and ran: ./node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser chrome. Source: programs/develop/plugin-special-folders/check-manifest-in-public.ts:19-24 pushes a WebpackError into compilation.errors, called unconditionally from plugin-special-folders/index.ts:88 whenever public/ exists.
findings.observed: The build did not ignore the file, it failed: "compiled with errors in 58 ms" then "Build error in manifest.json. / × manifest.json must not be placed under public/: .../legacy/public/manifest.json" and "Build failed with 1 error." Without public/manifest.json the identical project built cleanly.
findings.why: A reader carrying a public/manifest.json over from another toolchain is told the file is harmlessly ignored, so a red build with a manifest error looks like an unrelated bug. The page never mentions that the condition is a hard build failure, only a best-practice bullet later saying not to do it.

findings.docQuote: Read the [Extension.js contributing guide](https://github.com/extension-js/extension.js/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) to get set up and start contributing.
findings.evidence: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -L https://github.com/extension-js/extension.js/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md  ->  404. In the local checkout, `git ls-files | grep -i contributing` returns only docs/CONTRIBUTING.md; there is no CONTRIBUTING.md at the repository root.
findings.observed: HTTP 404. The tracked file lives at docs/CONTRIBUTING.md, so the working URL is https://github.com/extension-js/extension.js/blob/main/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md. The other three GitHub links on the same page (extension-js/docs, BACKERS.md, docs/TELEMETRY.md) all return 200.
findings.why: The page's single call to action for new contributors is a dead link, and it is the last line of the page, so a would-be contributor who follows it lands on a GitHub 404 with no obvious next step.

findings.docQuote: Silver sponsors and above also appear on the [front page](https://extension.js.org) and in the README. This page lists every tier.
findings.evidence: The same page lists TestMu AI under "### Bronze sponsors" (line 61) and its tier table gives Bronze only "Logo and link on this page and in BACKERS.md" (line 105) while Silver gets "Logo and link on the front page of extension.js.org and in the README on GitHub and npm" (line 106). But grep -in "testmu" on the site homepage (_FUTURE/extension.js.org/index.mdx:781-797) shows a TestMu AI tile inside the homepage Sponsors block, and grep -in "testmu" on the repository README.md:195-199 shows a TestMu AI logo block there too.
findings.observed: TestMu AI is documented as a Bronze sponsor yet is currently rendered both on the extension.js.org front page and in the GitHub README, which the page reserves for Silver and above. BACKERS.md also lists TestMu AI under "## Bronze sponsors" with Silver marked "_This tier is open._"
findings.why: The tier table is a price list. A prospective sponsor comparing $50 against $200 sees Bronze visibly getting the front-page and README placement the page says costs $200, so either the published benefits or the current placement is wrong and the reader cannot tell which.

findings.docQuote:
Your repository includes a Playwright configuration at:

- `playwright.config.ts`
findings.evidence: No create template ships a Playwright config: `find /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/programs/create -maxdepth 3 -name "playwright.config.*"` returns nothing, and the only example carrying one is the dedicated `playwright` example (_FUTURE/examples/examples/playwright/playwright.config.ts), which this page never mentions. The one playwright.config.ts at /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/playwright.config.ts belongs to the framework repo itself.
findings.observed: An Extension.js project created from any ordinary template has no playwright.config.ts. The claim also contradicts this page's own "Typical setup" section 200 lines earlier, which tells the reader to install @playwright/test and then "Create a `playwright.config.ts` and define browser projects and reporting."
findings.why: A reader is told a config already exists in their repository, goes looking for it, finds nothing, and cannot tell whether their scaffold is broken or a step was skipped. The sentence reads as leaked framework-repo context presented as a fact about the reader's project.

findings.docQuote: Family classification matches by substring, not by a closed list. Any browser name containing `chromium` classifies as Chromium-family, and any name containing `gecko` or `firefox` classifies as Gecko-family.
findings.evidence: programs/develop/lib/constants.ts:70-84 — isChromiumBasedBrowser returns `CHROMIUM_BASED_BROWSERS.includes(browser) || String(browser).includes('chromium')` and isGeckoBasedBrowser returns `GECKO_BASED_BROWSERS.includes(browser) || includes('gecko') || includes('firefox')`, where CHROMIUM_BASED_BROWSERS = ['chrome','edge','brave','opera','vivaldi','yandex'] and GECKO_BASED_BROWSERS = ['firefox','waterfox','librewolf'].
findings.observed: Classification is a closed list OR a substring, not a substring alone. Every fork the page names in its own prefix table classifies only via the closed list: 'brave', 'opera', 'vivaldi', 'yandex' contain no 'chromium', and 'waterfox', 'librewolf' contain neither 'gecko' nor 'firefox'.
findings.why: Taken at its word, the rule says brave and waterfox are in no family at all, contradicting the same page's table four sections earlier that grants them chromium:/firefox: keys. It also misleads anyone naming a custom target: an arbitrary name only inherits a family if it literally contains chromium, gecko or firefox, and the closed list is not extensible from user config.

findings.docQuote: ## Video walkthrough
findings.evidence: `wc -l docs/languages-and-frameworks/ecmascript-modules.mdx` reports 197 lines and `tail -8` shows the file ends immediately after this heading, with no <Frame>, no iframe, and no text. Every other page in this batch that promises a video (running-other-browsers.mdx:85, install.mdx:21, session-artifacts.mdx:35, chrome-devtools-mcp.mdx:23, playwright-e2e.mdx:108) carries a real youtube-nocookie <Frame> embed.
findings.observed: The page renders a "Video walkthrough" heading with nothing under it, so the section is an empty promise at the very bottom of the page.
findings.why: A reader who scrolls to the end, or jumps there from the table of contents, is told a walkthrough video exists and finds a blank section, with no way to know whether the embed failed to load or was never recorded.

findings.docQuote: If your setup is correct, Extension.js launches Chrome with a fresh profile, loads `github-search` as an unpacked extension, and prints a ready banner in your terminal. The Chrome address bar now recognizes `gh` as a keyword.
findings.evidence: extension create github-search (CLI 4.1.3) -> scaffolds the `javascript` template with src/manifest.json and src/background.js. Following Steps 2-3 literally (write manifest.json and service_worker.js, no path given, so at the project root) then running ./node_modules/.bin/extension build and reading dist/chromium/manifest.json.
findings.observed: Build succeeded but used src/manifest.json, not the tutorial's file. dist/chromium/manifest.json contains no "omnibox" key at all; it still declares the scaffolded sidebar template: {"name":"github-search","description":"Adds a sidebar panel to the browser with a simple page.","background":{"service_worker":"background/service_worker.js"},"action":{..."default_title":"Open Side Panel"},"side_panel":{"default_path":"sidebar/index.html"},"permissions":["sidePanel"]}. The emitted tree has no omnibox handler; background/service_worker.js is compiled from src/background.js. The root service_worker.js was never compiled.
findings.why: A reader following the flagship getting-started tutorial exactly gets the scaffolded sidebar demo, not a GitHub search extension. Typing `gh` in the address bar does nothing, and there is no error to explain why, because the files they were told to create are silently ignored. The page never says the manifest lives in src/ or that the scaffolded src/manifest.json must be replaced.

findings.evidence: cat github-search/package.json after ./node_modules/.bin/extension create github-search (CLI 4.1.3)
findings.observed: {"private":true,"name":"github-search","description":"Adds a sidebar panel to the browser with a simple page.","version":"1.0.0","license":"MIT","type":"module","scripts":{"dev":"extension dev","start":"extension start","build":"extension build","preview":"extension preview","build:chrome":"extension build --browser chrome","build:firefox":"extension build --browser firefox","build:edge":"extension build --browser edge"},"dependencies":{},"devDependencies":{"extension":"^4.1.3"}}
findings.why: The page presents this as the file the reader now has on disk. A reader comparing their scaffold against it sees extra scripts and a pinned "^4.1.3" instead of "latest", which makes it look like create misbehaved or that they scaffolded the wrong thing.

findings.docQuote: Under `--output json`, `preview` fails with `E_COMMAND_UNSUPPORTED_FOR_TARGET` (Safari is a supported browser, this command has no Safari path) and `start` fails with `E_UNSUPPORTED_BROWSER`.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension start --browser safari --output json  (CLI 4.1.3, run inside the scaffolded project)
findings.observed: {"schema":1,"ok":false,"command":"start","status":"usage","value":null,"error":{"code":"E_COMMAND_UNSUPPORTED_FOR_TARGET","message":"Safari is not supported by start."},"warnings":[]}  — the same code as preview, not E_UNSUPPORTED_BROWSER. `--browser webkit-based` returns the identical E_COMMAND_UNSUPPORTED_FOR_TARGET envelope.
findings.why: The page documents a machine-readable contract. A CI script or agent branching on error.code for `start` would never match E_UNSUPPORTED_BROWSER and would misclassify the failure as an unknown error instead of an unsupported-target refusal.

findings.docQuote: All Chromium-based and Gecko-based targets work on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Safari is the exception: it is supported on macOS only and requires full Xcode.
findings.evidence: docs/browsers/safari.mdx lines 113-118: "`extension build --browser=safari` works on Linux and Windows too: it produces the complete `dist/safari` web-extension bundle and **skips the Xcode packaging step** with a warning." Confirmed in CLI source at programs/extension/browsers/browsers-lib/messages.ts:669 (safariPackagingSkippedNonMac).
findings.observed: safariPackagingSkippedNonMac() emits: "Safari packaging needs macOS with Xcode, detected <platform>, so the Xcode packaging step is skipped. The web-extension build in dist/safari is still complete and can be packaged later on a Mac". The matrix's Safari row nonetheless shows ❌ under both Windows and Linux with no qualifier in those cells.
findings.why: A reader planning CI on Linux consults the matrix, sees ❌ for Safari on Linux plus "supported on macOS only", and concludes they cannot produce the Safari payload off a Mac. The tool actually does produce a complete dist/safari there, which is exactly the split-CI workflow safari.mdx recommends.

findings.docQuote: ## Video walkthrough
findings.evidence: wc -l docs/languages-and-frameworks/index.mdx -> 50; sed -n '44,50p' shows the file ends immediately after this heading with only a blank line.
findings.observed: The heading is the last content in the file. There is no <Frame>, no iframe, and no link following it, unlike every other docs page in this batch that has a video (e.g. docs/browsers/safari.mdx, docs/commands/logs.mdx), which embed a youtube-nocookie iframe under the heading.
findings.why: The heading renders in the page body and in the on-page table of contents, so a reader clicks through expecting a video walkthrough of the languages and frameworks support and lands on an empty section at the bottom of the page.

findings.docQuote:
Projects scaffolded with `create-extension` already silence this notice: the
generated `package.json` declares `pnpm.ignoredBuiltDependencies: ["less"]`,
which tells pnpm you have intentionally skipped the (no-op) script, so a single
install is clean with no `approve-builds` prompt.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension create less-check --template=new-less && cat less-check/package.json  (extension@4.1.3); plus grep -l ignoredBuiltDependencies _FUTURE/examples/examples/*/package.json
findings.observed: Scaffolded package.json contains only private/name/description/version/license/type/devDependencies{less,extension}/scripts/dependencies — no `pnpm` key at all. Across the whole template catalog: 0 of 53 example package.json files mention ignoredBuiltDependencies.
findings.why: A pnpm user is told the prompt is already handled by new scaffolds, so they will not add the key and will keep hitting the `Ignored build scripts: less` / approve-builds prompt the section exists to explain away.

findings.docQuote: A successful run prints a `status: "ready"` frame. Its `value` carries the project path and the list of previewed browsers.
findings.evidence: cd my-ext && ../node_modules/.bin/extension preview --no-browser --output json   (after a successful `extension build`)
findings.observed: {"schema":1,"ok":true,"command":"preview","status":"ready","value":{"browsers":["chromium"]},"error":null,"warnings":[]} — no project path field. `projectPath` appears only when a path argument is passed explicitly (`extension preview ./unpacked --no-browser --output json` -> value:{"projectPath":"./unpacked","browsers":["chromium"]}).
findings.why: A script that reads `value.projectPath` from the preview envelope gets undefined in the page's own documented default case ("If you omit the path, Extension.js uses the current working folder").

findings.docQuote: Every tool lives under the `extension_*` namespace, and the server ships 28 of them.
findings.evidence: npm i @extension.dev/mcp@10.9.0 (current latest) then a real MCP handshake: initialize + notifications/initialized + tools/list piped into node node_modules/@extension.dev/mcp/bin/extension-mcp.js
findings.observed: tools/list returns 30 tools. The package's own README line 10 also says "30 MCP tools".
findings.why: The count is the page's only quantitative claim about the server's surface, and a reader comparing it against `tools/list` output will think two tools failed to register.

findings.docQuote:
`preview` checks these locations in order:

1. `dist/<browser>` for the selected browser target.
2. The provided project path or current working folder.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension preview --help
findings.observed: Help lists a preview-only flag the page never mentions, in either the resolution order or the "Arguments and flags" table: `--output-path <dir>   path to an existing unpacked extension directory. Defaults to dist/<browser> when available`.
findings.why: The page presents an exhaustive flag table and a complete lookup order, so a reader wanting to preview an unpacked build outside the project never learns about the flag built for exactly that.

findings.docQuote: Nearly every Extension.js template ships a starter `STORE.md` generated from its own manifest; a couple of minimal templates do not, so add the file yourself if yours lacks one.
findings.evidence: for d in _FUTURE/examples/examples/*/; do [ -f "$d/STORE.md" ] || echo missing; done  (53 template dirs, 53 STORE.md, zero missing); confirmed live with three scaffolds: `extension create my-ext --template=content`, `--template=new-less`, and the bundled default `extension create default-check` — all three produced STORE.md
findings.observed: Every template in the pinned catalog ships STORE.md, including the minimal `init` template and the CLI-bundled `javascript` default.
findings.why: Sends readers hunting for a missing file, and understates a convention that is actually universal across the catalog.

findings.docQuote: - **Use `--polyfill` when needed**: Enable it only when your code depends on `browser.*` in Chromium-family targets.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension dev --help vs ./node_modules/.bin/extension build --help; source: programs/extension/commands/dev.ts:150 and programs/develop/command-build.ts:179
findings.observed: dev --help: "--polyfill [boolean]  whether or not to apply the cross-browser polyfill. Defaults to `true`" (same for start), while build --help says "Defaults to `false`". command-build.ts:179 comment: "`extension start` builds with commands.start values, polyfill on by default".
findings.why: The page frames the polyfill as strictly opt-in, so a developer who wants it off during development never learns they must pass `--no-polyfill` to `extension dev` / `extension start`.

findings.docQuote: ## Video walkthrough
findings.evidence: tail -8 _FUTURE/extension.js.org/docs/languages-and-frameworks/less.mdx
findings.observed: The heading is the last non-empty line of the file; no <Frame>, iframe, link, or text follows it.
findings.why: The page ends on a section promising a video that does not exist, unlike sibling pages where the same heading carries an embedded walkthrough.

findings.docQuote:
After the asset summary, a successful build prints two lines and stops:

```plaintext
⏵⏵⏵ Build succeeded with no warnings.
Your extension is ready for deployment.
```
findings.evidence: cd <sandbox>/ext-ts && ../node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chrome   (extension@4.1.3)
findings.observed:
⏵⏵⏵ Extension built for production in dist/chrome (59.1 KB).
⏵⏵⏵ Send this build to someone for review: https://docs.extension.dev/share/unpublished-build-for-review?utm_source=cli-build

Neither "Build succeeded with no warnings." nor "Your extension is ready for deployment." appears anywhere in the output. A build with one warning printed the same "Extension built for production" line, not "Build succeeded with 1 warning(s)."
findings.why: A reader or CI script that greps stdout for "Build succeeded" to confirm a green build never matches, so the check silently fails on every successful build.

findings.docQuote: The command prints no link and no next step. `build` is finished when the artifacts exist in `dist/<browser>`.
findings.evidence: cd <sandbox>/ext-ts && ../node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chrome   (extension@4.1.3)
findings.observed: The final line of a successful build is a link: "⏵⏵⏵ Send this build to someone for review: https://docs.extension.dev/share/unpublished-build-for-review?utm_source=cli-build". It is printed on every successful build, including under --output json (on stderr).
findings.why: The page states as a design guarantee something the CLI contradicts on every run, so a reader parsing the tail of build output, or auditing what URLs the tool emits, is told the wrong thing.

findings.docQuote: A successful run prints a `status: "built"` frame. Its `value` carries the project path, built browsers, the resolved mode, and one summary per browser.
findings.evidence: cd <sandbox>/ext-ts && ../node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chrome --output=json 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool
findings.observed: "value": {"browsers": ["chrome"], "mode": "production", "summaries": [{...}]}  — there is no project-path key anywhere in `value` (checked on both a clean build and a build with one warning). The other three items are present, and per-summary warning text is present as documented.
findings.why: A script reading the documented project path out of the envelope gets undefined, and has no way to attribute the frame to a project when several builds are run from one wrapper.

findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension build --help   (extension@4.1.3)
findings.observed: The CLI exposes a sixth Safari flag the table never mentions: "--development-team <id>  sign the Safari app with an Apple Developer team id (safari targets only). Without it the build is ad-hoc signed, which Safari treats as unsigned: the extension then needs Develop ▸ Allow Unsigned Extensions re-ticked on every launch. A signed build is listed and stays enabled across restarts".
findings.why: A reader who follows only this table ships an ad-hoc signed Safari app and hits an extension that disables itself on every browser restart, with no hint from the docs that a flag exists to fix it.

findings.docQuote: Extension.js **always merges** `.env.defaults` first when present, then the selected file's variables. Finally, **system** `process.env` takes highest precedence for overlapping keys.
findings.evidence: In one project (extension create ext-ts --template=content-typescript, which ships an extension.config.js): .env.defaults=EXTENSION_PUBLIC_API=fromdefaults, .env.chromium=EXTENSION_PUBLIC_API=fromchromium, .env=EXTENSION_PUBLIC_API=fromenv, manifest description "API is $EXTENSION_PUBLIC_API". Ran `extension build --browser=chrome` three times: as-is, with .env.defaults removed, and with extension.config.js removed.
findings.observed: As-is: dist/chrome/manifest.json -> "description": "API is fromdefaults" (EXTENSION_DEBUG=1 confirms the selected file is .env.chromium). With .env.defaults removed: "API is fromenv" — still not the selected .env.chromium. With extension.config.js removed: "API is fromchromium", matching the documented order. Cause: loading extension.config.* preloads .env.defaults then .env into process.env (programs/develop/lib/config-loader.ts preloadEnvFilesFromDir), and the bundler merge is `{...defaultsVars, ...envVars, ...process.env}`, so those preloaded values outrank the browser-scoped file.
findings.why: Every scaffolded template ships an extension.config.js, so for most readers a value set in .env.chrome/.env.chromium is silently overridden by .env.defaults or .env — the exact opposite of the documented precedence, and the build gives no warning that the browser-scoped value was discarded.

findings.docQuote:
Extension.js disables Node core fallbacks (for example, `crypto`, `path`, and `fs`) by default.

This means importing Node APIs may fail unless you add explicit fallbacks.
findings.evidence: Prepended `import * as path from 'path'` (then `import * as fs from 'fs'`) to src/background.ts of a scaffolded project and ran `../node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chrome`; compared with `buffer` and `os` imports.
findings.observed: `path` alone: exit 0, "⏵⏵⏵ Extension built for production in dist/chrome (59.5 KB)." — no error. `fs` alone: no error either (only the accompanying `os` import failed). By contrast `buffer` and `os` do fail with "Module not found: Can't resolve 'buffer'". The emitted dist/chrome/background/service_worker.js resolves path to an empty module (`var r={532(){}}` then `console.log(o(532).join("a","b"))`), so the call throws at runtime instead of at build time.
findings.why: The page's opening promise ("you see a resolution error at build time") and its two headline examples are wrong for `path` and `fs`: the build goes green and the extension throws once loaded in the browser, which is exactly the failure mode a reader consults this page to avoid.

findings.docQuote: If a project references `.scss`/`.less` files but the preprocessor is not installed, the build warns and ships the stylesheet as plain CSS instead of failing, matching how the browser loads whatever CSS it receives.
findings.evidence: Added src/content/extra.scss containing nested SCSS (`.foo { .bar { color: red; } }`), referenced it from manifest content_scripts[].css, and ran `../node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chrome` with no sass package installed.
findings.observed: The build's own warning contradicts "ships the stylesheet as plain CSS": "⏵⏵⏵ This Sass/SCSS file shipped uncompiled. ... The sass package isn't installed in this project. │ The raw Sass/SCSS source was copied as-is into the output .css. │ Browsers treat it as broken CSS, so those surfaces render unstyled. │ Install it to compile this file: npm install --save-dev sass"
findings.why: The doc's phrasing reads as a graceful degradation where styling still applies, so a reader may leave the warning unaddressed; the actual result is invalid CSS and an unstyled surface, which is what the CLI itself warns about.

findings.docQuote: | Content scripts    | Extension.js emits CSS as `content_scripts/[name].[contenthash:8].css` assets |
findings.evidence: Built a project whose manifest declares content_scripts[0].css = ["content/styles.css"] : `../node_modules/.bin/extension build --browser=chrome`, then listed dist/chrome and read dist/chrome/manifest.json.
findings.observed: dist/chrome/content_scripts/content-0.css (no content hash), and the emitted manifest points at "content_scripts/content-0.css". For comparison, hashed names do appear elsewhere in the same build (assets/icon.b4054220.png).
findings.why: A reader writing a cache-busting assumption, a CSP/web_accessible_resources rule, or a CI assertion against the documented hashed filename pattern will not match the file the production build actually emits.

findings.docQuote: The table ships as `extension-develop/contract/codes.json`, see [Result envelope](/docs/contracts/result-envelope).
findings.evidence: ls node_modules/extension-develop/contract/ ; find node_modules/extension-develop -name codes.json ; find /Users/cezaraugusto/local/extension-land/extension.js/programs -name codes.json -not -path '*/node_modules/*'
findings.observed: ls: node_modules/extension-develop/contract/: No such file or directory. The file is at node_modules/extension-develop/dist/contract/codes.json (and in the repo at programs/develop/dist/contract/codes.json). The documented path exists in neither the installed package nor the source tree.
findings.why: A consumer told to read the shipped table at that path finds nothing there and has to go hunting; the codes and mappings on the page are otherwise a faithful match for the real file (all 124 codes present, folded and legacy examples correct).

findings.docQuote:
`preview` expects existing build output.

- Run `extension build --browser=<target>`.
- Then run `extension preview --browser=<target>`.
findings.evidence: mkdir emptyproj; printf '{"manifest_version":3,"name":"e","version":"1.0"}' > emptyproj/manifest.json; ./node_modules/.bin/extension preview ./emptyproj --browser=chrome --output=json  (no dist/ anywhere)
findings.observed: Exit 0 with {"schema":1,"ok":true,"command":"preview","status":"ready","value":{"projectPath":"./emptyproj","browsers":["chrome"]},...}; ps shows the launched browser loaded --load-extension=<...>/emptyproj, i.e. the source manifest directory, not dist/chrome.
findings.why: Preview does not always fail without build output: it can fall back to loading the source directory, so a reader debugging "preview shows the wrong code" is pointed at a missing-dist theory when the real cause is that preview quietly ran unbuilt source.

findings.docQuote:
| `keepProfileChanges`  | Firefox only: persists changes made to the profile directory.            |
| `copyFromProfile`     | Firefox only: copies an existing profile before launching.               |
findings.evidence: programs/extension/browsers/run-chromium/chromium-launch/browser-config.ts:176-177 passes `keepProfileChanges: configOptions.keepProfileChanges` and `copyFromProfile: configOptions.copyFromProfile`; both are declared on the shared `BrowserOptionsBase` (programs/develop/types.ts:126,131), not on a Firefox-specific type, and are consumed by the shared helper programs/extension/browsers/browsers-lib/resolve-profile.ts:144-192. Confirmed in the published package: python scan of node_modules/extension/dist/browsers.cjs finds `keepProfileChanges: configOptions.keepProfileChanges` at two sites, one immediately following `getChromiumMasterPreferences`/`seedChromiumPreferences` (Chromium) and one following `getPreferences` (Gecko).
findings.observed: Chromium browserConfig in the shipped 4.1.3 bundle forwards both keepProfileChanges and copyFromProfile into resolveProfileConfig, which computes `const persisted = Boolean(persistProfile) || Boolean(keepProfileChanges)` for every engine.
findings.why: A reader targeting Chrome, Edge, or Chromium is told these two keys will not work for them and will reach for a hand-managed `profile` path or `persistProfile` instead, missing the seed-and-keep behavior the tool actually supports on their browser.

findings.docQuote: The Preact integration also uses optional packages such as `@prefresh/core`, `@prefresh/utils`, and `@rspack/plugin-preact-refresh`. When one is missing, the build error names the exact version that matches the bundled toolchain. The install command in the error is phrased for the package manager that your project uses.
findings.evidence: Read `maybeUsePreact` out of the installed node_modules/extension-develop@4.1.3 dist/0~rspack-config.mjs, and the source at programs/develop/plugin-js-frameworks/js-tools/preact.ts:36-93. Also grepped the bundle for the contract id: `preact-refresh` appears 8 times, all inside the `defineContract` literal in optional-deps-contracts, never at a call site.
findings.observed: The shipped maybeUsePreact resolves only preact/package.json, preact/compat, preact/test-utils, preact/jsx-runtime and preact/jsx-dev-runtime, then returns `{ plugins: [], loaders: void 0, alias }`. It never calls ensureOptionalContractPackageResolved, so the 'preact-refresh' contract is dead code and no missing-package build error can be raised. Separately, @prefresh/core@1.5.9, @prefresh/utils@1.2.1 and @rspack/plugin-preact-refresh@2.0.1 are hard entries in extension-develop's `dependencies`, so they are never absent either.
findings.why: The paragraph contradicts the disabled-fast-refresh note four lines below it and sends a Preact user chasing a nonexistent install step: they will add three packages that the toolchain neither requires nor loads, and will wait for an error message the CLI cannot emit.

findings.docQuote: the [contributing guide](https://github.com/extension-js/extension.js/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) is the entry point
findings.evidence: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://github.com/extension-js/extension.js/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md  →  404 (the same check returns 200 for blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md and for blob/main/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md). `git ls-files | grep -i CONTRIBUTING` in the repo lists only `docs/CONTRIBUTING.md`.
findings.observed: 404 for the linked URL; the file is tracked at docs/CONTRIBUTING.md, not at the repository root.
findings.why: This is the page's single call to action for would-be contributors, and it dead-ends on a GitHub 404 instead of the guide that actually exists one directory down.

findings.docQuote: Production builds (`extension build`) emit only the code your extension references plus a small reload runtime that is removed in production.
findings.evidence: cd scratch-ext && extension build --silent, then grepped every emitted script: `for f in $(find dist/chromium -name '*.js'); do grep -c -i 'reload' $f; done`
findings.observed: dist/chromium/background/service_worker.js: 0, dist/chromium/sidebar/index.js: 0, dist/chromium/content_scripts/content-0.js: 0 — the production output contains no reload runtime at all, so the sentence both adds and removes it in one clause.
findings.why: A reader auditing bundle contents for a store submission cannot tell from this sentence whether `extension build` ships reload glue, which is exactly the question the FAQ entry is titled to answer.

findings.docQuote: Keep the explicit-width pattern and test with `extension dev --browser=safari`; Safari is stricter about drawing before layout settles, so pre-sized containers matter more there.
findings.evidence: ./node_modules/.bin/extension dev --help  →  the -b/--browser entry reads "`safari` builds and opens a Safari app via Xcode (macOS only; no live reload)". The project's own Safari page states the same at docs/browsers/safari.mdx:25 ("`preview` and `start` are not available, and there is no live reload yet") and :43 (full Xcode app required, not just Command Line Tools).
findings.observed: `extension dev --browser=safari` requires macOS plus the full Xcode app and provides no live reload, none of which this page mentions.
findings.why: Ten lines earlier the page promises "Extension.js reloads the popup on save, which makes iterating on sizing fast"; a reader following the Safari advice on Linux or Windows cannot run it at all, and a macOS reader without Xcode hits a hard failure before any popup renders.
